newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Irish EU presidency seeks to avoid row at summit.
newsitem.headline: Irish EU presidency seeks to avoid row at summit.

text.p: European Union president Ireland, seeking to avoid a potential row at next week's summit in Dublin, is set to unveil a draft treaty for the 15-nation bloc that leaves out the most contentious items.

Diplomats said on Tuesday that issues such as the right to veto legislation, the number of European commissioners and a "flexibility clause" to allow some countries to integrate faster than others, would be dealt with only in brief commentaries.
Other potential changes to the EU's treaty will be presented to the bloc's leaders in draft legal form.
Ireland insists, however, that the draft treaty is only a working document, reflecting the progress made by negotiators since the EU began its inter-governmental conference (IGC) last March.

"We have not asked anyone to sign up to it as a treaty," Noel Dorr, chairman of the main negotiating group, said. "We have to ensure that those who hold very different views around the table have room to breathe."
Despite this, Britain indicated on Tuesday that it would head into the December 13 and 14 summit wary of plans for a "centralist, integrationist document".
At issue is a draft treaty ordered up by EU leaders in June in Florence as part of the bloc's preparations for a dozen or more new members from eastern Europe.
Although many differences exist among the 15 countries about what a new treaty should contain, Britain is the most isolated member, defending at all turns what it sees as attacks on its sovereignty.
Conscious of this, the Irish presidency is specifically designing a draft that the EU leaders can endorse without also endorsing the changes it suggests.

For example, it will contain a proposed treaty article on employment -- designed to make job creation an EU priority -- along with a commentary that recognises that some countries object to putting this in the treaty.
The proposed article, diplomats said, would reflect the general direction of the majority of countries.
But the Irish have steered clear of the main landmines, the veto, the Commission and flexibility.
Britain has said it will block any move towards further majority voting, a pledge reiterated in London on Tuesday by David Davis, Foreign Office minister for European affairs.

The flexibility clause, eagerly sought by France and Germany to stop countries such as Britain from holding back their plans for a closer union, is viewed with suspicion by Britain and a number of others which worry it is designed to leave them behind.
Small countries, meanwhile, refuse to countenance the loss of their European commissioner, a move some see as necessary if the bloc is to grow in numbers.
In all three cases, the Irish will simply describe the state of negotiations, diplomats said.
The approach will not suit all EU members. One diplomat told Reuters his country had been concerned that the Irish would write a report so bland "that even the British wouldn't kick up a fuss."
